subject: Critical Thinking
title: Conspiracy Theories: When Abduction Goes Wrong
description: A fast breakdown of Conspiracy Theories: When Abduction Goes Wrong for builders.

hook.text: A conspiracy theory IS an explanation. It just happens to be the worst possible form of abduction.

buildup.text: Good abduction: the simplest explanation that fits the evidence. Conspiracies: the most complex explanation possible.

discovery.text: Conspiracies violate Occam's Razor — they require thousands of people keeping perfect secrets forever.

twist.text: Real conspiracies (Watergate, Enron) get exposed quickly because humans can't keep secrets at scale.

climax.text: The appeal of conspiracy is abduction's weakness: any evidence can be 'explained' if you add enough layers.

punchline.text: If your theory explains everything, it explains nothing.

quiz.question: Why do conspiracy theories violate Occam's Razor?

details.summary: Conspiracy theories are a form of abductive reasoning gone wrong: they select explanations based on narrative appeal rather than evidence, parsimony, or testability. They exploit the brain's preference for intentional explanations.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding how conspiracy theories misuse abductive reasoning equips you to evaluate extraordinary claims without dismissing legitimate concerns.
takeaways: Conspiracies prefer complex intentional explanations over simpler ones
They violate Occam's razor by adding unnecessary hidden agents
Self-sealing design makes them immune to disconfirmation

faq.question: How do conspiracy theories misuse the logic of abductive reasoning?
faq.answer: They select explanations that feel satisfying narratively rather than those best supported by evidence, and they introduce unnecessary hidden agents that violate parsimony.

faq.question: What logical feature makes conspiracy theories particularly resistant to debunking?
faq.answer: They are unfalsifiable by design: any evidence against them is reinterpreted as part of the conspiracy, making it impossible for any evidence to count against the theory.
